acceptance.criterion: Cost math fixtures and complete recurring categories
acceptance.expected: Units and full-snapshot multiplication tested; primary rates or explicit unknowns
acceptance.observed: 415 local Python tests pass (one full run after source de35a7c1b324eaf691935eb840b0c488894e3c56, none skipped; 371 before the fixture receipt script added its own) and 63 Go tests pass in the offline fixture package (one run on the same source), including cost units, retention, receipt, measurement-validation, S3 unit, S3 request-model, readiness-cadence, egress, restore and headroom tests; focused golangci-lint reports 0 issues. Five deliberate regressions (a 10^9 storage divisor, a 300 s readiness cache, KMS requests set equal to S3 requests, inbound write bytes counted as egress, multipart ignored) each fail the suite. Rates for EC2, EBS, T4g credits, KMS, Secrets Manager, IPv4, CloudWatch and S3 storage are read from AWS's own US West (Oregon) price lists, each with a receipt file, rate code, source hash and publication date checked against the rate table by the tests; no numeric rate changed. S3 request prices, data transfer and the Resend prices stay labeled unverified. S3 storage is priced in GiB-months: the S3 pricing page defines 1 GB as 2^30 bytes (hashed receipt, corroborated by the price list's 1,024-based tier boundaries), so snapshot bytes convert by 2^30 and the full-mix storage line falls 6.87% (from 298.95 to 278.42 USD); product quotas stay decimal bytes and no other AWS unit was re-based. S3 requests are counted per object size at the AWS CLI defaults (8 MiB threshold and chunk): 1,145 requests a backup for the full mix instead of 32, from a labeled per-object size assumption, with the KMS ratio an explicit one-per-object assumption and the per-request ratio an unverified sensitivity outside every subtotal. Embeddings are reported as the gateway's cl100k service counter, provider call counts (readiness 28,800 to 43,200 embeds on a 30-day month, derived from Caddy's 30 s probe and the service's one-minute cache, not measured) and average proxies; provider tokens, restore and reopen frequency, the recall response size and outbound bytes beyond recall responses stay unknown and no bound is invented. Egress is an average unbounded by the current plan. Measurements use an owned schema and are validated (no booleans, negatives, NaN, oversized or wrongly typed values, wrong containers or unattributed records); a bad record returns BLOCKED, and a record changes only its own scenario. The schema accepts no embedding token, database size or egress field because no producer can attest their provenance. The full mix counts all 29 allowed brains (32 backup objects). Each scenario reports a peak exposure: T4g surplus credits 46.72 USD at sustained 100% CPU and 29.20 USD at 70% mean, KMS key storage 3 USD after two rotations, no global free allowance. Full-limit known subtotal is $305.47/month and its peak is $353.34/month; neither is a full maximum or an authorized quote. The CPU credit mode is unverified, and control database lifetime growth, embeddings, restore and reopen re-embeds, log and metric volumes, S3 request inputs, response size, outbound bytes and peak email volume are unknown, so launch cost qualification is NOT_QUALIFIED.

acceptance.expected: Finite caps, production guards, real outcomes and full workload evidence
acceptance.observed: CLI --live is deliberately disabled before manifest/credential reads/network, returning BLOCKED/exit 2 with a zero-call receipt; a test proves a fully valid manifest, credential directory and running loopback server see zero requests. The candidate client is tested against a real loopback HTTP server for: per-request outcomes over all offered requests (status BLOCKED/FAIL/PARTIAL, never COMPLETE); one wall-clock deadline per exchange (0.6s budget, first byte at 0.5s then a stall: 0.604s measured, 1.105s before the fix) that also covers hostname resolution in a disposable child killed and reaped at the deadline (0.4s budget with a stalled lookup: 0.401s measured, 2.008s before; an IP-literal origin starts no child); a cap check before every socket operation with queued-work cancellation; strict finite budget; byte-based token precharge with an operator-declared provider-work bound; canonical origins; fixed error classes with no credential prefix leak; confirmed-only session cleanup; a completed TLS exchange, default certificate verification, a TLS stall, and hostname-not-IP certificate matching and SNI through the resolver are covered with throwaway certificates. The deadline keeps a 0.25s scheduling tolerance and is a client-side guarantee checked against local sockets, not observed behavior of a live target. The independent review's findings are repaired and each is covered by a test that failed first: a gateway tool error is decoded from the parsed result into a fixed enum (capacity and operation_in_progress count as admission rejections, quota and client faults are kept apart, only a not_found answer to a forget of an id this run remembered is a durability error, an unknown code is never reflected); the elapsed preflight counts readiness, per-account setup, the final drain and cleanup (8,535 s for the frozen workload against an 8,100 s schedule); a malformed or deeply nested initialize reply still yields a sanitized receipt and closes the issued session, a close failure cannot discard results, and an integer past 2^63-1 is an invalid budget; a failure measured on dispatched requests is FAIL even when another cap stopped the run, and a run whose shortfall comes only from never-dispatched arrivals stays BLOCKED; the fact vocabulary keeps the frozen 32 to 512 word range under the gateway's 4,096-byte limit (at most 4,095 bytes, no truncation). Word counts are nominal, not provider-billed tokens. Still open: the hot-tenant rate-limit decision (decision-request-hot-tenant-rate-limit.md), the eligible-traffic versus saturation decision (decision-request-full-cardinality-eligible-traffic.md), a service run over the seeded state (the offline fixture exists and is verified, but four seams are open), a real cold-open workload, host telemetry, isolation probes, reviewer freeze and a separately authorized real run (live-enable-requirements.md). Offline fixture preparation (evals/hosted-load/fixtureprep, fixture-preparation.md, fixture-receipt.json): a full fixture of 14 accounts, 29 brains and 90,000 canonical memories, each account at its plan memory cap, was prepared from real hosted code and verified by an independent read-only command that regenerates the expected facts, cross-checks the control database, the canonical files, the store projection and the index, and runs the gateway's own Inventory and Entitlement on a scratch copy of the control database (30 checks, all pass). The same 90,000 facts hash to one content digest across two complete full preparations (64-wide and 1,536-wide vectors, both batched), and a second reading in stdlib Python (fixture_recount.py) reproduces that digest from the files. A third full preparation with one commit per fact stopped at brain 15 of 29 (see limitations), so per-write history is measured only on the 15 brains that finished. A separately labeled reduced smoke (290 memories, 29 brains) never satisfies the full cardinalities. Missing, corrupt, swapped, interrupted and mismatched fixtures fail closed (Go negative fixtures and a command-line transcript). The fixture is infrastructure only: vectors come from a hash embedder, so provider and retrieval quality stay unqualified; it fills the memory count and no storage quota; every account is at its memory cap, so the gateway refuses further remembers; 25,002 of the 90,000 facts are reachable by the current load client; no service ran over it. Four seams block a service run (integration-request-fixture-service-seams.md).

acceptance.expected: Named T23.41 review before execution; measured capacity supports published limits
acceptance.observed: Reviewer/date remain unset. Simulator is mechanics-only and no real provider or deployed-capacity run occurred. With the gateway's real fixed window the frozen hot tenant (120 requests a minute) is refused 180 of 7,379 steady requests (2.44%), above the 1% admission limit, on a healthy server; no number was changed and the decision is open with the task41 reviewer and the T23.45 admission owner. The full advertised cardinality (every account at its plan memory cap, 90,000 memories over 29 brains) cannot be eligible steady traffic under the frozen 15%/5% mix: a deterministic inventory replay shows the gateway's memory-count rule alone refusing 726 of 7,379 steady remembers (9.84% of all offered), and the current client refusing 1,130 and skipping 396 forgets. Chief-architect's PR #239 ruling classifies correctly enforced quota refusals as expected boundary outcomes: retain them in total/offered outcomes and exclude them from the unexpected-admission denominator; it does not change the 90,000 cardinality, traffic mix, plan limits or capacity status. No number changed, and the exact eligible-versus-boundary sample decision remains open with the task41 reviewer (decision-request-full-cardinality-eligible-traffic.md).

limitations: No supported live-load execution: CLI is fail-closed until live-enable-requirements.md is satisfied. The candidate client has loopback-server tests only and never reports better than PARTIAL.

The per-exchange deadline covers hostname resolution (a disposable child, killed and reaped at the deadline), connect, TLS, headers and body under one monotonic deadline, within a 0.25s scheduling tolerance plus child start and post-deadline SIGTERM/SIGKILL/reap time (up to 1.2s if a child survives SIGTERM and SIGKILL). It runs the host's operating-system resolver unmodified, tries addresses sequentially, and adds one child (20-37ms measured locally) to each hostname exchange's recorded latency. It is checked against local sockets and a scripted resolver only; it says nothing about a live target or DNS provider.

Token precharge is encoded argument bytes (an upper bound, no tokenizer verified), plus an operator-declared provider_work_bound for server-side work the client cannot observe. The committed manifest leaves that bound null, so a live run stays blocked.

No provider calls or deployment occurred. No complete cost or capacity qualification is claimed. Deadline and resolver tests are timing-based against real sockets and child processes and could flake on a heavily loaded host.
Backup lifecycle model assumes about 60 days of full timestamped snapshots and needs measured/architecture validation; its full-limit exposure exceeds the historical $60 ceiling.

Workload word counts are nominal sizes of synthetic text, not gateway-metered or provider-billed tokens; no tokenizer is assumed. The gateway meters with its own tokenizer, so real token use per request can differ from the nominal figure.

The frozen hot tenant offers the gateway's 120 requests-per-minute account limit. The simulator's limiter reproduces the gateway's fixed window that starts at an account's first request and the 600 per minute address limit, but counts offered arrivals only, so live counts can differ by a few requests per window from setup and cleanup requests. Rejections are counted as failures, not excluded.

Every request sends Connection: close and pays a fresh TCP and TLS handshake, and latency runs from dispatch, not from the scheduled arrival, so client-side queueing behind the eight workers is not in the recorded p95. Read latency and handshake-load figures with both in mind.

The rate table is primary-verified for the AWS rates listed in the receipts. S3 request prices and data transfer out (with its 100 GB allowance, decimal GB assumed) are unverified against a regional catalog, and the Resend prices are a vendor page. Backup object sizes (an even share of each account's storage quota bytes), mixes, usage fractions, the AWS CLI multipart defaults, the one-KMS-request-per-object ratio, the recall response average and shared-account free allowances (the 20,000 KMS requests and the transfer allowance) remain assumptions; provider price and tokens, log volumes, custom metrics, restore and reopen activity, retries and aborts remain unknown. The two AWS documentation receipts (S3 storage unit, CLI multipart defaults) are hashed pages fetched once from the public sites; no AWS account API was called.

The peak exposure is a sensitivity, not measured usage and not a full maximum. The T4g credit mode is unverified (the template sets no CreditSpecification; unlimited mode bills surplus credits, standard mode throttles). The control database is copied whole into every snapshot and the runtime never prunes it; its lifetime growth (about 156 USD a month of added backup storage after a year at full usage, from the sampled write and recall slope plus readiness rows) is a sensitivity outside every subtotal and needs a dbstat measurement. The retention baseline is the deployed template's; a thinning proposal is unapproved and not modeled.
No load-client output carries cost measurements, and T23.68's command passes load.json to --measurements, which returns BLOCKED; see integration-request-cost-measurements.md.

The readiness cadence (60 to 90 s spacing) is derived from the Caddy interval and the service cache, and no call count is measured. The egress line is an assumed average; the plan does not bound the recall response size, and this task implements no cap. Neither an average nor a service-counter total is a bound on provider-billable tokens, because the candidate provider's tokenizer is unqualified.

The cardinality headroom replay models the gateway's memory-count rule only (no limiter, storage rule, monthly cap, faults, cold opens, races or latency) and is not a measured runtime failure. The storage and history gap is separate: the fact text of a full plan is at most 4.096% of its storage quota. The offline fixture measured its own Git history and derived-index sizes (fixture-receipt.json), which is a fixture measurement and not the production maximum: production history, its pinned provider's vector width and real usage are unmeasured.

The offline fixture (fixture-preparation.md) is infrastructure only. Its vectors come from a hash embedder pinned as fixture-hash-embedder-d64@infrastructure-only-v1 (the width is a fixture parameter, not the provider's), paid entitlements are direct SQL in the fixture's own control database, legacy ids are sequential, Git history is batched (one commit per 500 facts) except in a labeled 100-per-brain per-write sample and a partial per-write measurement on the 15 brains that finished in a full preparation that stopped (no whole-fixture per-write history exists), and its subscriptions expire 30 days after preparation. Two hazards were observed and are not root-caused: a writer lock briefly retained by a forked Git child (the preparer retries), and one per-write brain whose HEAD commit object vanished under this host's Git (Apple Git 2.54.0, automatic maintenance suspected, not reproduced in a scratch check); no runtime code changed. Prepare times were measured while other preparations ran on the same host and are indicative only. No service, provider, cloud or network call occurred.
